summary: The best general-population data for pushing is the Cooper Institute bench-press-to-bodyweight norms: men 20-29 median is about 1.0-1.06x bodyweight (p20 0.88, p80 1.32, p95 1.63; ACSM-style p10-p90 0.80-1.48), and women 20-29 median about 0.65x (p20 0.51, p80 0.80; p10-p90 0.48-0.90), falling to roughly 0.45x by 50-60+ for women and to under 1.0x even at the 95th percentile for men 60+. Cooper samples are health-conscious clinic clients, so true population values (including people who cannot bench the empty bar) are probably lower, especially in the bottom tail. Untrained-study baselines agree: untrained young men bench about 60 kg (130 lb) and women about 42 kg (92 lb). CSEP/CPAFLA push-up norms put a 'good' (about 40-59th pct) young man at 22-28 full push-ups and a young woman at 15-20 knee push-ups, with steep decline by age; a self-report poll suggests about half of US adults cannot do 10 push-ups. I found no usable general-population or untrained-baseline numbers for overhead press, machine chest press, dumbbell press or dips in result snippets; these will have to be modelled from bench via ratios.
